titre: Florence, 1966: The Flood That Sped Up Art Restoration
accroche: On November 4, 1966, the water rises to the halo of Cimabue's Christ in Florence, and Italian and foreign volunteers rush in.
contenu_vulgarise:
## The Water Rises

On November 4, 1966, the Arno overflows in Florence. In the Santa Croce neighborhood, the water tops 6.7 meters. In the basilica's museum, the great Crucifix painted by Cimabue in the thirteenth century is submerged up to the height of Christ's halo. The wood soaks up oil, mud and naphtha, swells, warps and cracks the paint; as it recedes, the water carries off about 60% of the paint layer. Farther on, the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, on the banks of the Arno, is cut off from the rest of the city: about 1.3 million items, a third of its holdings, are damaged, including most of the works in the Palatine and Magliabechi collections.

## The Improvised Rescue

Florence is not prepared for such a disaster. Volunteers pour in from Italy and abroad, students, restorers, book specialists: the press nicknames them the *angeli del fango*, the mud angels. According to The Art Newspaper, most of the work on the ground is nevertheless done by Italian conservators and volunteers; foreign help brings mainly funds and extra staff. Sending the books to other institutes is considered, then ruled out on logistical grounds. Rescued volumes are washed and disinfected, then dried in the libraries when space allows, or outside the city, in tobacco kilns and granaries. Blotting paper is slipped between the pages and replaced when saturated; in the kilns, humidity is lowered slowly from ninety to forty percent. For fear of mold, everything is done as fast as possible.

## A Discipline Picks Up Speed

Within six months, the library has 144 people at work, eighty-one of them student volunteers. The team develops a nine-step repair method that lets them process between seventy and a hundred books a day. Specialists such as the British bookbinder Peter Waters put their knowledge to work on the project; the techniques he devises in Florence become the basis of the Library of Congress's conservation program, where he is chief of conservation from 1971 to 1995. Notions such as "phased conservation" and methods such as mass deacidification are conceived during this period.

Cimabue's Crucifix is entrusted to a team led by Umberto Baldini and Ornella Casazza. For ten years, they reapply the paint in an almost pointillist manner, with the help of computer modeling; the tiny flecks of pigment that fell into the water are recovered with pliers. The work is back on display in 1976.

The Florentine restoration laboratory, founded in 1932 by Ugo Procacci within the Superintendency and the first modern restoration laboratory in Italy, expands into the Fortezza da Basso because of the number of works to treat. In 1975, the Ministry of Culture merges the Opificio delle Pietre Dure's laboratories, the Superintendency's and other small Florentine laboratories to create today's institute. The flood also sped up the adoption of techniques such as heat-set tissue repair and mass deacidification, which became standard in research libraries. Decades later, the sources note, work remains to be done.

repere.texte: At the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, about 1.3 million items, a third of the holdings, are damaged by the flood of November 4, 1966.

carte.punch: In 1966, the Arno flood forces Florence to improvise a rescue that speeds up restoration.
carte.idee: On November 4, 1966, the Arno floods Florence: about 1.3 million items of the Biblioteca Nazionale and Cimabue's Crucifix are hit. Italian and foreign volunteers improvise the rescue; phased conservation and mass deacidification are conceived in this period.

quiz.question: Why did the 1966 Florence flood advance art restoration?
choix: Because all the damaged books and paintings were sent abroad, where better-equipped workshops treated them
Because foreign volunteers did most of the work on the ground, without the help of Italian restorers
Because Cimabue had left written instructions on how to restore his work
Because the scale of the damage gave rise, in an emergency, to methods that became common practice
quiz.explication: The city was unprepared: shipping the books abroad was ruled out on logistical grounds, and most of the work on the ground was done by Italian conservators and volunteers, with foreigners bringing mainly funds and reinforcements. Phased conservation and mass deacidification were conceived in this period, not from instructions left by Cimabue.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which British bookbinder sees the techniques developed in Florence become the basis of the Library of Congress's conservation program?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Peter Waters, a British bookbinder, later heads conservation at the Library of Congress; Baldini and Casazza led the restoration of Cimabue's Crucifix, and Procacci founded the Florentine restoration laboratory in 1932.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Baldini and Casazza's team reapply the lost paint of Cimabue's Crucifix?
choix: With a uniform repaint, in a single tone, over all the lost areas
By replacing the lost areas with photographs of the work
In an almost pointillist manner, with the help of computer modeling
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The team works for ten years, in an almost pointillist manner and with computer modeling; the work is back on display in 1976.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what year does the Ministry of Culture merge the Florentine laboratories to create today's Opificio delle Pietre Dure?
choix: 1966, the same year as the flood
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The merger of the Opificio's laboratories, the Superintendency's and other small Florentine laboratories dates from 1975, nine years after the 1966 flood.
